home.name: Francis Desjardins
home.enough: A dependency is easy to add and hard to remove, and most of what one does goes unused. The cost of adding one never arrives on the day you add it.

skills.title: What I build
skills.description: Framework-free cores with thin bindings over them: the core is plain TypeScript that runs in a browser, a worker or a service, and the binding is the only part that knows which — a test walks the import graph and fails if the core ever reaches a framework.
skills.thinking: A state library and a draft engine, to hold a few plain objects, is a cannon aimed at a fly: a set of listeners and a shallow compare do the same work, nine kilobytes lighter. Some problems are the other way round — time zones, cryptography, anything whose hard part is the one you have not met yet. Between the two, a library earns its place the day the requirements outgrow what you wrote.
skills.secondary: Also: a self-declared cat person. The cats have yet to object.

work.title: What's running
work.description: Four pieces, each with a surface you can try. The names come from an eclipse: the three shadows it casts, and the beads of light that break through at its edge. What they refuse to do is documented as carefully as the rest.

dialog.name: antumbra
dialog.description: Dialog manager on the native top layer. Zero shipped UI: the renderer stays yours. React, Solid and vanilla bindings.

boot.name: umbra
boot.description: Bootstrap orchestration, and not a front-end kind: the core needs no DOM, so one declared graph boots a page, a worker or a service. You say what each step needs; the parallelism is derived from that — no flag, no concurrency ceiling.

designSystem.name: penumbra
designSystem.description: The design system all four playgrounds wear — and the page that takes it apart, one layer at a time.

bead.name: bead
bead.description: A binary call protocol in TypeScript and C#, at parity, with a builder that generates both sides from a .proto. It covers requests, subscriptions at the client's pace, transfers, cancellation, payload rules, and the same calls over HTTP and JSON with their OpenAPI document. Here the server runs in a Web Worker of the page.
